name: Battle of Iwo Jima
info: American Marines, Navy and Army forces landed on Iwo Jima in the Volcano Islands in February 1945 and took it from the Japanese garrison under Kuribayashi in five weeks, at a cost in casualties higher than the Japanese suffered.

facts.place: The island of Iwo Jima in the Volcano Islands, Japan, with its two airfields (South Field and Central Field) and Mount Suribachi at the southern end
facts.sides: The United States Marine Corps, Navy and Army (Operation Detachment) under Admiral Raymond A. Spruance, Vice Admiral Richmond Kelly Turner, Lieutenant General Holland M. Smith and Major General Harry Schmidt, with about 60,000 Marines in the battle; the Imperial Japanese Army and Navy garrison of 21,060 men under Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi
facts.outcome: The Americans captured the island, which was declared secure on 26 March 1945. Of the 21,000 Japanese on the island at the start, only 216 were taken prisoner, and more than 26,000 Americans were casualties, including 6,800 dead.

t: Kuribayashi rejected the usual Japanese defence of the beach and built defences in depth, with 18 km of tunnels dug by the time of the landing and positions that could be reoccupied after they had been cleared.

Total American casualties exceeded Japanese casualties, in a ratio of three American casualties for every two Japanese, which was unique among Pacific War battles involving amphibious island landings.

Whether the island's capture was worth its cost has been disputed since April 1945, and the airfield's value as a base for fighter escorts and for emergency landings by B-29 bombers is still argued over.
dyk: The photograph of the flag-raising on Mount Suribachi shows the second of two flag-raisings there on 23 February 1945. The first flag was replaced by a larger one, and the photograph won the Pulitzer Prize for Photography in the year it was published.
ev: Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi is assigned to command the defence of Iwo Jima, and the American air raids and shore bombardment begin on 15 June
Marines land on the south-eastern beaches, and by the evening 30,000 have come ashore
A patrol raises the American flag on Mount Suribachi, and the second, larger flag is photographed by Joe Rosenthal
Captain Samaji Inouye's 1,000 men charge the American lines, and the 3rd Marine Division reaches the northern coast
The island is declared secure at 09:00 on 26 March after a final Japanese counterattack the night before
The 147th Infantry Regiment spends three months clearing the Japanese who still hold out in caves and tunnels
Two Japanese holdouts surrender, nearly four years after the battle

sections.background:
After the American capture of the Marshall Islands and the air attacks on Truk Atoll in January 1944, Japanese military leaders reassessed their position. They set up an inner line of defences running north from the Carolines to the Marianas and on to Japan through the Volcano Islands, and in March 1944 the Japanese 31st Army under General Hideyoshi Obata was activated to garrison it. After the American conquest of the Marianas, bombers flew daily from there against mainland Japan, and Iwo Jima served as an early warning station that radioed reports of incoming bombers to the home islands.

The loss of the Marianas in the summer of 1944 raised the importance of the Volcano Islands for the Japanese, who feared that losing them would ease American air raids, disrupt war manufacturing and damage civilian morale. The Combined Fleet had lost almost all its striking power in the latter half of 1944, and aircraft based in the home islands could not support Iwo Jima, since their range was not more than 900 km. Japanese staff officers later described a strategy of delaying the enemy with the defences already built while the defence of the homeland was prepared.

After the battle of Leyte, the Allies had a two-month lull before the planned invasion of Okinawa. Iwo Jima gave the Japanese an air base from which to intercept B-29 bombers on their way to Japan, and they used it to stage intermittent air attacks on the Marianas from November 1944 to January 1945. American intelligence was confident that the island would fall in one week, and the invasion was codenamed Operation Detachment.
sections.forces:
The American force was the Fifth Fleet under Admiral Raymond A. Spruance, with the Joint Expeditionary Force under Vice Admiral Richmond Kelly Turner and the Expeditionary Troops under Lieutenant General Holland M. Smith. Major General Harry Schmidt commanded the V Amphibious Corps: the 5th Marine Division (25,884 officers and enlisted men) on the southern beaches, the 4th Marine Division (24,452) on the northern ones, and the 3rd Marine Division (19,597) in floating reserve, with the 147th Infantry Regiment (2,952). About 450 American ships lay off the island, and the battle involved in all about 60,000 Marines and several thousand Navy Seabees.

The Japanese had 21,060 men under arms. Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi, assigned to the command in June 1944, knew that his garrison could not win, but hoped to inflict such casualties that the United States and its allies might reconsider invading the home islands. Drawing on the defence of Peleliu, he built defences in depth, not on the beach: mutually supporting fortifications linked by tunnels, with hidden artillery and mortar positions, and Takeichi Nishi's tanks camouflaged as static artillery. By 19 February 18 km of a planned 27 km of tunnels had been dug. His superiors ordered some beach defences against his wishes. Supplies were short: 60% of the ammunition normally thought sufficient for one engagement by a division, and food for no more than four months.

Major General Schmidt asked for ten days of bombardment before the landing, then nine. Rear Admiral William H. P. Blandy, who needed time to replenish his ships' ammunition, insisted on three, which was resented among the Marines.
sections.course:
The first wave of Marines landed on the south-eastern beaches at 08:59 on 19 February. The landings soon became congested in the loose volcanic ash, and the Japanese, who had held their fire for just over an hour, opened up with machine guns, mortars and heavy artillery shortly after 10:00. The ash was too soft for foxholes or for the amtracs to climb, and bulldozers of the Seabees eventually cut roads off the beach. The 28th Marines drove across the island at its narrowest, about 800 m, and cut off the Japanese on Mount Suribachi. At the Quarry on the right flank, the 3rd Battalion of the 25th Marines landed about 900 men and had 150 fit for fighting by nightfall. By evening 30,000 Marines had landed.

Kuribayashi had forbidden the usual night banzai charges. The Marines found firearms relatively ineffective and used flamethrowers and grenades, and flame-throwing Sherman tanks proved highly effective. A kamikaze attack on 21 February sank the escort carrier USS Bismarck Sea. Suribachi was cut off by 23 February, and a patrol raised the flag there. In the north the Marines faced the Motoyama Plateau, Hill 382, Turkey Knob and the Amphitheater, which they called the meatgrinder. They attacked Hill 362 at night without a barrage, and on 8 March Captain Samaji Inouye and his 1,000 men charged, inflicting 347 casualties (90 deaths); the Marines counted 784 Japanese dead. The 3rd Marine Division reached the northern coast the same day.

The island was declared secure at 18:00 on 16 March. On 21 March the Marines destroyed Kuribayashi's command post in a gorge with four tons of explosives, and on the night of 25 March a force of 300 Japanese attacked near Airfield No. 2. The island was officially declared secure at 09:00 on 26 March.
sections.aftermath:
According to the Navy Department Library, the 36-day assault resulted in more than 26,000 American casualties, including 6,800 dead. Of the 21,000 Japanese on the island at the start, only 216 were taken prisoner, some of them only because they had been knocked unconscious or otherwise disabled. Most were killed in action, though 3,000 or more went on resisting in the cave systems after the main fighting ended. Two Marines were captured during the battle, and neither survived captivity. Because all civilians had been evacuated, there were no civilian casualties.

After the island was declared secure, the 147th Infantry Regiment spent three months digging the Japanese out with flamethrowers, grenades and satchel charges. It killed some 1,602 Japanese soldiers in small actions, along with many others who died in sealed caves, and captured 867, while suffering fifteen killed and 144 wounded. Two of Lieutenant Toshihiko Ohno's men held out for four years and surrendered on 6 January 1949.

Of the ships hit by the kamikaze attack of 21 February, USS Bismarck Sea was sunk, the last American aircraft carrier lost in the Second World War, and USS Saratoga was so badly damaged, with the loss of 132 men, that she took no further part in combat or transport duties. The kamikaze attacks killed 318 American sailors. By comparison, the 82-day Battle of Okinawa cost over 62,000 American casualties, over 12,000 of them killed or missing.
sections.sources:
The Japanese side is known in part from Japanese Monograph No. 48, a postwar study in which Japanese staff officers described the strategy of the defence. The beach landing is described by participants and observers, among them the Time-Life correspondent Robert Sherrod, and by historians such as Derrick Wright. Figures for American casualties come from the Navy Department Library, and J. Robert Moskin records the fighter sorties flown from the island. Six Navajo code talkers under Major Howard Connor, the 5th Marine Division's signal officer, sent and received over 800 messages without error in the first two days.

Some points are disputed. Accounts from surviving Japanese veterans conflict over the final attack on the night of 25 March, and it is possible that Kuribayashi led it in person, which would have made him the highest-ranking Japanese officer to lead an attack in person in the war. Popular press accounts published after the flag photograph had the Marines fighting all the way up Mount Suribachi, but the patrol that climbed it met only a few defenders. Three Marine Corps investigations changed the names of the men in the photograph: in 1946 and 1947 Harlon Block was found to have been wrongly identified as Henry Hansen, in 2016 John Bradley was found not to be in it and Harold Schultz to be, and in 2019 Rene Gagnon was found not to be in it and Harold Keller to be. The island's strategic value is also disputed.
sections.legacy:
The necessity and long-term significance of the capture have been contentious since the battle. In April 1945 the retired Chief of Naval Operations William V. Pratt wrote in Newsweek of a small island useless to the Army as a staging base and useless to the Navy as a fleet base. The airfield supported P-51 escort fighters, but only ten escort missions were flown from Iwo Jima, and Moskin records 1,191 fighter escorts and 3,081 strike sorties against Japan. There were 2,251 B-29 landings on the island. Robert Burrell argues that the emergency-landing justification became prominent only after the capture, and that of the nearly 2,000 B-29s that landed from May to July 1945 more than 80% did so for routine refuelling. The lessons of Iwo Jima guided the planning of the Battle of Okinawa, where the preparatory bombardment was made the heaviest yet delivered on a Pacific island.

Medals of Honor went to 22 Marines (12 posthumously) and five sailors, four of them hospital corpsmen, 28% of those awarded to Marines in the war. Felix de Weldon's Marine Corps War Memorial, taken from Rosenthal's photograph, was dedicated at Arlington on 10 November 1954. American and Japanese veterans met on the island in 1970, and on 19 February 1985 a Reunion of Honor was held on the landing beach, where a memorial carries inscriptions in both languages and the two sides shook hands. The Japanese government continues to search for and retrieve the remains of its dead.

summary: From 19 February to 26 March 1945 American Marines, with Navy and Army support, took Iwo Jima from a Japanese garrison of about 21,000 under Kuribayashi, who had fortified it in depth with tunnels. More than 26,000 Americans were casualties, and the island's value has been disputed ever since.

Richard F. Newcomb, Iwo Jima (Bantam Books, 1982)
Whitman S. Bartley, Iwo Jima: Amphibious Epic (Historical, Division of Public Information, Headquarters, United States Marine Corps, 1954)
Kumiko Kakehashi, So Sad to Fall in Battle: An Account of War Based on General Tadamichi Kuribayashi's Letters from Iwo Jima (Presidio Press, 2007)
Derrick Wright, The Battle for Iwo Jima 1945 (Sutton Publishing, 2007)
Bill D. Ross, Iwo Jima: Legacy of Valor (Vintage, 1986)
notes: Japanese casualties: the article gives no total. It says casualties were three American to two Japanese, and also that Japanese combat deaths were three times American KIA; I gave only the 3:2 ratio and the 216 prisoners. These do not fit neatly with 21,000 garrison and 6,800 US dead.
The lead says 21,000 Japanese; the order of battle says 21,060 under arms; both used.
The 147th's 867 captured plus its dead is said to be over 10% of the garrison; left out.

Kamikaze: the 21 February attack is called the only one of the battle, yet the planning section says kamikazes killed 318 American sailors during the battle; I used both as the article gives them and did not reconcile them. Another statement that 40 sailors died on USS Blessman is left out.
The article's section on Medal of Honor says 22 Marines and five sailors; used.

The flag-raising text is garbled in places (Gagnon described as a runner in the second raising); I kept only the Rosenthal photo, 23 February, the Pulitzer and the identification changes. 'Pulitzer in the year of its publication' as article says.

Garbled: the Navajo code talkers section's paragraph is a patchwork of quotations; I used only the 800 messages and Connor's six from the landing section. Names 'Yamakage Kufuku [sic]' and 'Matsudo Linsoki [sic]' left out.

Left out: the table of damaged ships (empty in the text), the flamethrower technical details and designations, the Marine Corps reverence claim (Burrell), Smith's remarks, casualty detail of Roselle, the dedication of the ships named USS Iwo Jima and Iwo Jima Day.
The article's hint that the Japanese attack at the Quarry and 3rd Battalion figure (83.3%) is kept as 150 of 900 fit.
